sources.claim: HRW dispatch (2026-03-26): India's parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill 2026, which removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court judgment, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups (hijra, kinner) plus intersex individuals — excluding self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people — and mandates medical certification for identity recognition. HRW calls it a major setback that strips thousands of rights and increases risk. As national law it sets the recognition baseline for visitors and residents across every Indian state and union territory, including this one.

BBC News (2026-03-26): parliament approved in both houses an amendment to the 2019 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act that redefines transgender identity and removes the self-identification right; it awaits presidential assent. Opposition parties and the LGBTQ community protested; the government says the change makes welfare benefits more accessible, while critics say it excludes transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people. The piece recalls the 2014 Supreme Court 'third gender' ruling and reports recognition remains uneven amid continuing discrimination in education, healthcare and formal employment — the national baseline that applies in this region.

records.name: Mizoram
records.current_summary:
No Mizoram-specific trans statute or enforcement record is on file; the union of national law governs recognition here. In March 2026 that national framework narrowed significantly: both houses passed an amendment to the 2019 trans persons law removing self-identification, restricting legal recognition to biologically-verified and traditional-community categories, and mandating medical-board certification for gender-affirming surgery. The bill drew nationwide protests from the community and opposition parties, a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw it, and presidential assent remained pending as of late March 2026.

Neither international reporting on the change nor any other source on file records Mizoram-level deviation — statute, ban, or enforcement campaign — in either direction; the northeast state's day-to-day exposure for a trans visitor therefore runs through the central framework, its pending narrowing included.
records.current_localsOnly: Mizoram is one of the 12 states/UTs that have constituted the transgender welfare board under the 2020 national rules; an RTI investigation found most such boards are 'rudderless' - without a policy framework, compliance mechanism or real power. All boards are resident-facing service bodies with no visitor-facing function.

sources.claim: HRW report (26 Mar 2026): India's parliament passed the 2026 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill narrowing the 2019 law: it removes self-identification, restricts legal recognition to traditionally recognised groups (hijra/kinner) and intersex persons, and requires medical certification for identity recognition — reversing the 2014 Supreme Court ruling. The bill adds offences including up to life imprisonment for 'coercing or alluring' anyone to be transgender, which HRW warns could criminalise support networks. Of 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons, only about 32,500 hold identity cards. HRW urges the president not to sign; assent pending as of late March 2026.

BBC (26 Mar 2026): India's parliament passed an amendment to the 2019 transgender-rights law replacing self-identification with recognition based on biological or physical traits plus traditional identities (hijra/kinner-style); medical boards and district authorities must now certify gender-affirming surgery. The government says the narrower definition targets welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics warn it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling; presidential assent is pending. India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

records.name: Manipur
records.current_summary:
Manipur sits under India's national framework with no region-specific trans statute, ban or enforcement campaign reported. That framework narrowed on 26 March 2026: both houses passed an amendment to the 2019 Transgender Persons Act removing the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricting legal recognition to historically recognised communities (hijra/kinner) and intersex people, and requiring medical-board certification — with a new offence carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing someone into transition per human-rights reporting. Recognition is already thin in practice: about 32,500 of the census-recorded 487,803 transgender persons hold ID cards. A court-appointed advisory panel sought withdrawal amid protests; assent was pending.

The country dossier's reporting on the amendment explicitly notes no Manipur-specific deviation — the recognition machinery, the certification requirement and the new offence apply to the state exactly as elsewhere in India, which is what sets a visitor's exposure there.
